meta.title: The Country-Sized Zone That No Longer Exists on Any Map
meta._convention: Duration omitted per beat -- filled from measured narration length. The Saudi-Iraqi Neutral Zone (1922-1991) is a historical jurisdiction, not a country in the map dataset -- highlight stays [] throughout for every beat; its kite-shaped outline is hand-drawn with `lines` around its real center (~29.125N, 45.521E, Uqair Protocol 1922, ~7,044 sq km, partitioned 1981-82 and formally dissolved by 1991), per the pipeline's 'scenes that aren't a country' pattern. Iraq and Saudi Arabia (both real countries, both present in country-codes.json) are labeled via markers only, kept un-highlighted so the gold accent stays reserved for the zone itself. The zone's exact historical boundary is approximated schematically for the animated outline -- not a survey-accurate polygon.

beats.voText: For most of the 20th century, this desert belonged to no country. It was a neutral zone between Iraq and Saudi Arabia.
In 1922, British and Saudi negotiators created it so nomadic tribes could cross the desert freely, no fences, no checkpoints, no fixed border.
The Neutral Zone covered about 7,000 square kilometers, roughly the size of a small country, belonging to neither Iraq nor Saudi Arabia.
beats.onScreenText: 7,000 sq km, owned by no one.

beats.voText: By the 1980s, oil interests and modern border politics made a shared no-man's-land impossible to maintain, so both countries agreed to just split it.
The zone was divided in 1982 and formally dissolved by 1991, absorbed so completely that it doesn't appear on any modern map at all.
A country-sized piece of desert that belonged to no one, quietly erased by two governments and a straight line on a map. Follow for more places on Earth that shouldn't exist, but do.
